session: 2026 Oklahoma Legislative Session (adjourned sine die May 14, 2026)

bills.title: Data Center Customer Ratepayer Protection Act of 2026
bills.lastAction: Approved by Gov. Stitt on May 11, 2026. In effect as of July 1, 2026. Requires large-load customers (75+ MW) to pay for new grid infrastructure, mandates separate tariffs with credit requirements, and requires developers to notify the Corporation Commission, county commissioners, and neighboring property owners within 60 days of buying land for a project.
bills.votes: 92-2 (House); 46-0 (Senate); final version, after House and Senate negotiators settled their differences: 84-0 (House), 48-0 (Senate)
bills.policyRelevance: Ensures data center operators bear proportional costs for grid infrastructure upgrades rather than passing them to residential ratepayers. Defines large-load customers as 75+ MW facilities. Now the tariff framework the Oklahoma Corporation Commission must apply to the first live loads. Covered in depth in Issue #17 (The Meter Goes Live) and Issue #19 (The Gate).

bills.title: Water and water rights; establishing procedures for permitting, monitoring, and reporting of groundwater use
bills.lastAction: Signed by Gov. Stitt May 20, 2026. Takes effect November 1, 2026. Filed in 2025 and passed in 2026. Final language defines penalties for failure to report groundwater usage, allows a groundwater permit for a data center's cooling only if the system is closed-loop or another low-consumption design that recirculates the water, and creates a complaint process through the Oklahoma Water Resources Board.
bills.policyRelevance: The water-side companion to HB 2992's cost-attribution floor: metering and closed-loop cooling for large-load data centers. Of direct relevance to Phoenix Wells and geothermal procurement, since enhanced geothermal does not consume the cooling-tower water cycle most hyperscale data centers rely on. Covered in Issue #15 (Water on the Meter).

bills.title: Data privacy; establishing consumer rights; appeal process; privacy notice; data protection assessments; penalties; liability
bills.lastAction: Approved by Gov. Stitt on March 20, 2026. Takes effect January 1, 2027. Filed in 2025: the Senate passed it 46-0 in March 2025, the House passed it 84-4 on February 19, 2026, and the Senate accepted the House version 38-7 on March 16, 2026.
bills.policyRelevance: Oklahoma's first comprehensive consumer data privacy law, joining roughly twenty states with comprehensive frameworks: gives residents rights over personal data collection, sale, and deletion by companies.

bills.title: Oklahoma Responsible Technology in Schools Act
bills.lastAction: Approved by Governor May 12, 2026, with emergency clause. Requires every district to adopt a written AI policy before the 2027-28 school year; mandates educator-directed, human-in-the-loop AI use; prohibits AI as the primary basis for grading, discipline, or placement; preserves parents' right to opt students out of student-facing AI tools without academic penalty.
bills.policyRelevance: Sets a statewide floor for AI governance in K-12: district policies, human oversight, a ban on high-stakes AI decisions, and family transparency. One of the first state frameworks of its kind.

bills.title: Crimes and punishments; modifying elements of certain unlawful acts; aggravated identity theft; effective date
bills.lastAction: Became law without the Governor's signature on May 7, 2026. Takes effect November 1, 2026. Creates aggravated identity theft and makes it a crime to use a stolen or made-up (synthetic) identity, with intent to defraud, to get money or property. Anyone who uses artificial intelligence, among other digital tools, to commit identity theft faces additional penalties on top of the identity theft charge.
bills.policyRelevance: With SB 1734, one of the AI-related bills that became Oklahoma law in 2026. It does not regulate AI itself; it names AI as a tool of identity theft and raises the penalty for using it that way.

bills.title: Artificial intelligence; definitions; requiring operators make certain disclosure; preventative measures for minor account holders; prohibitions; enforcement authority to Attorney General; civil penalty
bills.lastAction: Passed the Senate 43-0 on March 23, 2026. The House passed an amended version 90-0 on April 28 and sent it back to the Senate on April 29. The Legislature ended its session on May 14 before the Senate voted on the House changes, so the bill died. It does not carry over; it would have to be refiled in 2027. Correction, October 26, 2026: this entry said the bill was enacted. It was not.
bills.policyRelevance: No legislator voted against it in either chamber, and it still died: the calendar ran out, not the votes. The House's version would have required operators of AI chat services used by minors to provide parental controls and to send users who mention self-harm to crisis services.

bills.title: Technology; artificial intelligence; companions; minors; safety; civil penalties
bills.lastAction: Passed the House 96-0 on March 25, 2026. The Senate Technology and Telecommunications Committee approved an amended version on April 16, and it was placed on the Senate floor calendar on April 21, but the full Senate never voted on it. It died when the session ended May 14. Bills not enacted by the end of the 2026 session (the second session of the 60th Legislature) are dead and do not carry over.
bills.policyRelevance: House companion to SB 1521 (the same two authors). It would have barred making social AI companions knowingly available to minors and required safety protocols for users. Neither bill became law in 2026.

bills.title: Corporation Commission; requiring implementation of certain standards
bills.lastAction: Sent to the Senate Rules Committee on February 3, 2026, and never heard there. It died when the session ended May 14, 2026, and would need to be refiled in 2027.
bills.policyRelevance: Would have directed the Corporation Commission to set standards that prioritize affordable, reliable, and clean energy security, including preferences for fuel sources produced in the United States. Watch for a 2027 refile.

bills.title: Well Repurposing Act
bills.lastAction: Passed the House 85-6 on March 16, 2026. The Senate Energy Committee approved an amended version on April 23, and it was placed on the Senate floor calendar on April 28, where it stayed. It did not get a Senate vote by the May 7 deadline for bills from the other chamber. Dead for the 2026 session and does not carry over.
bills.policyRelevance: Would have converted abandoned oil and gas wells into geothermal energy sources. Strong House support but no Senate floor vote before deadline. Directly relevant to Phoenix Wells; a 2027 refile is the path forward.

bills.title: Public utilities; defining terms; requiring certain public utilities to make certain filing with Corporation Commission
bills.lastAction: Sent to the House Appropriations and Budget Committee on February 4, 2026. Its Natural Resources Subcommittee recommended it 9-0 on February 16, but the full committee never acted, so it never reached the House floor. It died when the session ended May 14, 2026.
bills.votes: 9-0 (House Appropriations and Budget Natural Resources Subcommittee)
bills.policyRelevance: Would have required utilities to add a surcharge for large-load data center customers and sent the money to a new Grid Modernization Revolving Fund. The cost-attribution ground it aimed at was partly covered by HB 2992, which did become law.

bills.title: Crimes and punishments; creating and disseminating a digitization or synthetic media; making certain acts unlawful
bills.shortTitle: AI Deepfakes and Political Ad Disclosure
bills.lastAction: Approved 6-0 by the House Criminal Judiciary Committee on February 17, 2026, and 13-0 by the House Judiciary and Public Safety Oversight Committee on February 26, both times in a rewritten version (a committee substitute). The full House never voted on it, and it died when the session ended May 14, 2026. Correction, November 2026: this card earlier listed this topic under SB 1890, which is an unrelated bill. HB 3299 is the 2026 bill on this subject.
bills.votes: 6-0 (House Criminal Judiciary); 13-0 (House Judiciary and Public Safety Oversight)
bills.policyRelevance: Would have made it a crime to create and share AI-made or digitally altered media using a real person's name, image, voice, or likeness without written consent, with intent to cause harm: a misdemeanor, or a felony above $25,000 in financial harm or when used for extortion. Political ads using such media to show a candidate would have had to say so before an election (the bill sets a 45-day period). Rep. Hays filed a similar bill, HB 3073, in 2024; it passed the House 81-15 and stalled in the Senate.

bills.title: Artificial intelligence; prohibiting distribution of certain media and requiring certain disclosures
bills.lastAction: Filed in 2025. Approved 5-2, as amended, by the Senate Technology and Telecommunications Committee on February 27, 2025, and placed on the Senate floor calendar on March 4, 2025. The full Senate never voted on it in 2025 or 2026, and it died when the session ended May 14, 2026. Correction, November 2026: this card earlier listed this topic under HB 4012, which is the state budget bill. SB 894 is the bill on this subject.
bills.policyRelevance: Would have barred knowingly spreading an AI deepfake of a candidate or party on the ballot within 90 days of an election unless it carried a clear label saying the image, audio, or video was manipulated or generated by AI. Candidates could go to court to stop it, with fines of up to $1,000, $5,000, or $10,000 depending on the case. The penalties were civil, not criminal.

bills.title: Health Insurance; requiring certain decisions to be made by licensed professional; prohibiting issuance of outcomes determined with artificial-intelligence; requiring disclosure notice by insurer
bills.lastAction: Sent to the Senate Business and Insurance Committee on February 3, 2026, and never heard there. It died when the session ended May 14, 2026. Correction, November 2026: this card earlier listed this topic under SB 1650, which is an unrelated bill, and named a Senate Insurance Committee, which does not exist. SB 2038 is a 2026 bill on this subject.
bills.policyRelevance: Would have required a licensed health care professional to issue any final denial or other adverse decision by a health insurer, barred adverse decisions that come from an AI system unless such a professional reviewed them, required a disclosure notice from the insurer, let the Insurance Commissioner examine insurers' AI systems, and set a $10,000 fine per violation. Two other 2026 bills on AI in health insurance decisions also died without a hearing: SB 1967 (Sen. Mann) and HB 3675 (Rep. Provenzano).
